CHAPTER 2.2 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.2 · LEARNING AREA 2 · MARCH

Multi-stage random experiments

A component passes through three inspection stations, two balls are drawn from an urn, a test decides what is sorted out. Such experiments happen in stages. With the tree diagram and two simple path rules you keep track. You also learn when two events are independent and why that is not the same as mutually exclusive.

9 LESSONS3 UNITSTREE DIAGRAMSQUALITY CONTROL
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • apply the multiplication rule for independent events and prove stochastic independence by calculation
  • represent multi-stage random experiments as a tree diagram
  • calculate with the product rule and the sum rule for paths, with and without replacement
  • solve problems from quality control, tests and selection procedures

COIN AND DICE

A coin and a dice are thrown at the same time.

  • Write down all the outcomes. How many are there?
  • How likely is “heads and six”? Find a calculation that needs no counting.

DRAWING TWICE

  • How likely are two red balls? And one of each colour?
  • What changes if the first ball is put back?

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Multiplication rule and independence

Coin and dice together have $2 \cdot 6 = 12$ equally likely outcomes. “Heads and six” is one of them, so $P = \tfrac{1}{12}$. That is exactly $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac16$. The coin knows nothing about the dice: the probabilities are simply multiplied.

Two events that do not influence each other are called independent. Whether this is the case cannot always be seen at first glance. You check it by calculation with the multiplication rule.

KEY POINT · STOCHASTIC INDEPENDENCE

Two events $A$ and $B$ are called stochastically independent if $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$ (multiplication rule).

Intuitively: whether $A$ occurs or not makes no difference to the probability of $B$. If the equation does not hold, $A$ and $B$ are dependent.

Independent is not mutually exclusive: mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are always dependent, because $P(A \cap B) = 0 \neq P(A) \cdot P(B)$.

Typically independent: throws with different devices, repeated throws, drawing with replacement.

Typically dependent: drawing without replacement, features of the same person such as age and height.

INTERACTIVE · INDEPENDENT OR NOT?

Set $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A \cap B)$. In the square on the left: if the share of $A$ inside $B$ is as large as outside it, the events are independent.

EXAMPLE 1 · SURPRISINGLY INDEPENDENT

Dice: $A$: “even”, $B$: “at most 4”. Are $A$ and $B$ independent?

$P(A) = \tfrac12$, $P(B) = \tfrac46 = \tfrac23$, $A \cap B = \{2, 4\}$, so $P(A \cap B) = \tfrac26 = \tfrac13$.

$\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac23 = \tfrac13$: independent, although both depend on the same roll.

EXAMPLE 2 · DEPENDENT

Dice: $A$: “even”, $C$: “at most 3”. Are $A$ and $C$ independent?

$P(A) = P(C) = \tfrac12$, but $A \cap C = \{2\}$, so $P(A \cap C) = \tfrac16$.

$\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14 \neq \tfrac16$: dependent.

EXERCISES

a) Two coins: how likely is “both heads”?   b) Coin and dice: how likely is “tails and an odd score”?

a) $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$   b) $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$

We have $P(A) = 0.4$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. Are $A$ and $B$ independent if a) $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$   b) $P(A \cap B) = 0.3$?

$P(A) \cdot P(B) = 0.2$. a) independent   b) dependent

A device consists of two components that work independently of each other, with probabilities 98% and 95% of working. How likely do both work? How likely does at least one fail?

$0.98 \cdot 0.95 = 0.931$. At least one fails: $1 - 0.931 = 0.069$.

Dice: are $A$: “prime number” and $B$: “even” independent?

$A = \{2, 3, 5\}$, $B = \{2, 4, 6\}$, $A \cap B = \{2\}$. $\tfrac16 \neq \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12$: dependent.

Show: if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive and $P(A) > 0$ and $P(B) > 0$, then $A$ and $B$ are dependent. Explain the result in words as well.

$P(A \cap B) = P(\emptyset) = 0$, but $P(A) \cdot P(B) > 0$. In words: if $A$ occurs, you know for certain that $B$ does not occur. That is the strongest form of dependence.

TEST YOURSELF!

How likely is “heads and six” when throwing a coin and a dice?

$\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac16$

Two independent components work with 98% and 95%. How likely do both work?

$0.98 \cdot 0.95$

$A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, both with positive probability. Then they are …

$0 \neq P(A) \cdot P(B)$

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Tree diagrams and path rules

The bag contains 3 red and 2 blue balls. The first ball is red with $\tfrac35$. After that there are still 2 red and 2 blue ones in it: the second one is then red with $\tfrac24$. For “both red” you multiply: $\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 = \tfrac{3}{10}$.

A tree diagram shows each stage as a branching. Every way from the root to a leaf is a path and stands for an outcome. On the branches you write the probabilities that hold in that situation.

KEY POINT · PATH RULES

At every node the probabilities of the outgoing branches add up to 1.

1st path rule (product rule): the probability of a path is the product of the probabilities along the path.

2nd path rule (sum rule): the probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of its paths.

With replacement the probabilities stay the same from stage to stage, without replacement they change.

Check: all the path probabilities together add up to 1.

Shortcuts: you do not always have to draw the whole tree. Often the paths that belong to the event, or the complementary event, are enough.

INTERACTIVE · TREE DIAGRAM WORKSHOP

Set up the urn, choose 2 or 3 draws, with or without replacement. Tap the ends of the paths or choose an event: the path rules calculate along with you.

EXAMPLE 3 · WITHOUT REPLACEMENT

3 red, 2 blue balls, two draws without replacement. How likely are two different colours?

Two paths: red–blue $\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 = \tfrac{6}{20}$ and blue–red $\tfrac25 \cdot \tfrac34 = \tfrac{6}{20}$.

Sum rule: $\tfrac{12}{20} = \tfrac35$

EXAMPLE 4 · WITH REPLACEMENT

The same urn, two draws with replacement. How likely are two red balls, how likely is at least one blue ball?

$P(\text{red, red}) = \left(\tfrac35\right)^2 = \tfrac{9}{25} = 0.36$.

At least one blue is the complementary event: $1 - \tfrac{9}{25} = \tfrac{16}{25} = 0.64$

EXERCISES

A coin is tossed three times. Draw the tree. How likely are exactly two heads?

Three paths $HHT$, $HTH$, $THH$ with $\tfrac18$ each: $\tfrac38$.

An urn contains 4 white balls and 1 black ball. Two draws are made without replacement. How likely is the black one among them?

black first $\tfrac15$, or white then black $\tfrac45 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac15$: together $\tfrac25$.

A spinner shows red with probability 0.3. It is spun twice. How likely is red exactly once?

$0.3 \cdot 0.7 + 0.7 \cdot 0.3 = 0.42$

From a class with 10 girls and 15 boys two people are drawn by lot. How likely are they two girls, how likely one girl and one boy?

Two girls: $\tfrac{10}{25} \cdot \tfrac{9}{24} = 0.15$. Mixed: $2 \cdot \tfrac{10}{25} \cdot \tfrac{15}{24} = 0.5$.

At least how often must you roll a dice so that the probability of at least one six is greater than 90%? Use a table of values on the graphing calculator.

$1 - \left(\tfrac56\right)^n > 0.9$. Table: $n = 12$ gives about $0.888$, $n = 13$ about $0.907$. So at least 13 times.

TEST YOURSELF!

3 red, 2 blue balls, two draws without replacement: how likely are both red?

$\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24$

Coin three times: how likely are exactly two heads?

$3 \cdot \tfrac18$

$P(\text{red}) = 0.3$, two spins: how likely is red exactly once?

$2 \cdot 0.21$

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Quality control, tests and selection procedures

Imagine 10,000 parts. 500 of them are faulty, and the inspection device detects $0.98 \cdot 500 = 490$. Of the 9,500 good ones it wrongly sorts out $0.01 \cdot 9500 = 95$. So 585 parts are sorted out, and only $\tfrac{490}{585} \approx 84\%$ of them are really faulty.

Calculating with such natural frequencies is often easier than with percentages. They correspond exactly to the path rules: every number in the tree is the count on that path.

KEY POINT · STRATEGIES

Tree diagram if the process happens in stages. Two-way table if two features are considered at the same time.

Natural frequencies: calculate with 1,000 or 10,000 imagined cases, then form proportions.

Calculate “at least one” almost always via the complementary event “none”.

For a question such as “What proportion of the parts sorted out is faulty?”, only the group of parts sorted out goes into the denominator.

Series and parallel: two components in series work if both work. In parallel, one is enough. More on this in switching algebra in the chapter “Outlooks”.

INTERACTIVE · HOW RELIABLE IS A POSITIVE TEST?

Set how common a feature is and how well the test works. The two-way table and the tree show what proportion of those who test positive really have the feature.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE INSPECTION DEVICE

Solve the exploration “Sorted out” with probabilities.

Sorted out: $0.05 \cdot 0.98 + 0.95 \cdot 0.01 = 0.049 + 0.0095 = 0.0585$.

Proportion faulty among those sorted out: $\tfrac{0.049}{0.0585} \approx 0.838$, i.e. about 84%.

EXAMPLE 6 · THREE SELECTION STAGES

A selection procedure has three stages, passed by 60%, 50% and 80% of the participants, independently of each other. How many of 200 get through?

$0.6 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.8 = 0.24$.

$200 \cdot 0.24 = $ 48 people

EXERCISES

On a car, the paintwork is faulty with probability 2% and the engine with probability 1%, independently of each other. How likely is a car free of faults?

$0.98 \cdot 0.99 = 0.9702$

A test has 4 questions with 3 answers each, exactly one of which is correct. For someone guessing: how likely are all correct, how likely is at least one?

All: $\left(\tfrac13\right)^4 = \tfrac{1}{81}$. At least one: $1 - \left(\tfrac23\right)^4 = \tfrac{65}{81} \approx 0.80$.

1% of the population has a disease. A test detects 90% of those who are ill, but is also positive for 5% of the healthy. How likely is someone with a positive test really ill? Calculate with 10,000 people.

100 ill, 90 of them positive. 9,900 healthy, 495 of them positive. $\tfrac{90}{90 + 495} = \tfrac{90}{585} \approx$ 15%. Check with the widget.

A basketball player scores a free throw with 70%. How likely does she score at least once in two throws?

$1 - 0.3^2 = 0.91$

Two components each work with 90%, independently of each other. How reliable is a series connection, how reliable a parallel connection?

Series: both must work, $0.9^2 = 0.81$. Parallel: it only fails if both fail, $1 - 0.1^2 = 0.99$.

TEST YOURSELF!

In example 5, what proportion of the parts sorted out is really faulty (three decimal places)?

$\tfrac{490}{585} \approx 0.838$

How likely do you guess all 4 questions with 3 answers each correctly?

$\left(\tfrac13\right)^4$

How reliable is a parallel connection of two components with 90% each?

$1 - 0.01$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Two dice: how likely are two sixes? Calculate with the multiplication rule and check with the table from chapter 2.1.

$\tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac16 = \tfrac{1}{36}$, one cell out of 36 in the table.

Connecting with chapter 2.1: an urn contains 2 red and 3 green balls. Two draws are made with replacement. How likely are both the same colour?

$0.4^2 + 0.6^2 = 0.16 + 0.36 = 0.52$

A dice is rolled until a six comes up, but at most three times. How likely does the six come up?

Complementary event: no six three times, $\left(\tfrac56\right)^3 = \tfrac{125}{216}$. So $1 - \tfrac{125}{216} = \tfrac{91}{216} \approx 0.42$.

Five tickets, one of them wins. Two people draw one after the other without replacement. Is it an advantage to draw first?

First: $\tfrac15$. Second: the first person draws a blank ($\tfrac45$), then the second draws the winner ($\tfrac14$): $\tfrac45 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac15$. No advantage.

EXCURSIONA FAMOUS DISPUTE

The Monty Hall problem

In a game show there are three doors. Behind one is a car, behind each of the other two a goat. You choose a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens another door with a goat and asks: “Do you want to switch?”

In 1990 the columnist Marilyn vos Savant answered: switching doubles the chance of winning from $\tfrac13$ to $\tfrac23$. Thousands of readers contradicted her, including people with doctorates. She was right. The tree shows it: with $\tfrac23$ you are standing in front of a goat at first, and then switching leads to the car for certain. Try it out.

Source: Marilyn vos Savant, column “Ask Marilyn”, Parade Magazine, 9 September 1990.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

INDEPENDENCE

$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$. Mutually exclusive with positive probabilities means dependent.

Dice: “even” and “at most 4” are independent

TREE DIAGRAM

Each stage a branching, the branches at a node add up to 1.

Urn: $\tfrac35$ red, then $\tfrac24$ red

PATH RULES

Multiply along a path, add the paths of an event.

different colours: $\tfrac{6}{20} + \tfrac{6}{20} = \tfrac35$

WITH AND WITHOUT REPLACEMENT

With: the same probabilities at every stage. Without: they change.

red twice: $0.36$ with, $0.3$ without replacement

APPLICATIONS

Natural frequencies, complementary event for “at least”, the right reference group in the denominator.

Inspection device: $\tfrac{490}{585} \approx 84\%$
